title: The far side of the Moon isn’t dark: it gets as much sunlight as the side we see

cover.alt: The grey, fully lit far side of the Moon in front of a blue Earth swirled with white clouds, seen from deep space.

body: The Moon is **tidally locked**: it turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to orbit Earth, so the same face always points at us. The hidden hemisphere was nicknamed the dark side because it was unseen, not because it is unlit. On average both halves get almost equal amounts of direct sunlight, and the whole far side is in night only when we see a full Moon. It also looks different: battered with craters and almost free of the dark lava plains that mark the face we know.

slides.alt: Time-lapse from deep space: a grey Moon slides from left to right across the face of a cloudy blue Earth, showing its sunlit far side.
slides.caption: July 2015: from about a million miles (1.6 million km) out, the camera on NASA’s DSCOVR satellite sees the Moon cross in front of Earth, its far side lit by the Sun.

slides.heading: The dark side of the Moon

left.label: Myth
left.text: One side of the Moon never sees the Sun.

right.label: Fact
right.text: Both sides get almost equal sunlight on average. “Dark” meant unseen: most of it was never seen until 1959.

slides.heading: Share of each side covered by dark lava plains
slides.note: The plains are the maria, or ‘seas’; with so few, the far side is the brighter one

slides.prompt: On a night under a ‘full Earth’, the near side of the Moon gets about 10 lux of earthshine. How dark is a far-side night?
slides.detail: Earthshine on the near side is about as bright as a pavement under streetlights, and 34 times brighter than a full Moon on Earth.

slides.question: When is the whole far side of the Moon in night?
options: When we see a full Moon
When we see a new Moon
slides.explanation: At full Moon, the Sun is lighting the face turned towards us, so the far side has its night. At other phases, part or all of it is in daylight.
